text: Nine lessons, one continuous thread, no detours. This last lesson steps back and looks at the whole thing at once — what got built, and what changes next.

In order: a clarified requirement, turned from a vague Slack message into one real sentence. A plan, naming six Snowflake objects before writing any SQL. A warehouse and a load, small and auto-suspending, loading data with a load that fails loudly instead of quietly. A summary query at the right grain. A role built with least privilege from day one. A view that query lives behind. A Power BI connection in import mode. And a two-minute presentation, with exactly two visuals.

Look at that list again, and one thread runs through every single choice. An XS warehouse, because the workload is genuinely tiny. A view instead of a table, because nothing demanded the extra complexity of a refresh job. Import instead of DirectQuery, because nothing needed real time. One role instead of a governance framework, because there was only one stakeholder. None of those were shortcuts — each one was the correctly sized answer for this specific ask.

The Intermediate project picks up exactly where one stakeholder stops being true. Add a second stakeholder asking a related but different question, and several of these simplifications stop being enough. One role becomes several, each scoped narrowly. A manual COPY INTO becomes a real pipeline built on Streams and Tasks, because someone remembering to run a load by hand stops being good enough. And a flat CSV becomes semi-structured JSON, which is where Snowflake's VARIANT type and the FLATTEN function come in.

But notice what doesn't change at all. Clarify the real ask before building anything. Name your objects before creating them. Grant only what's actually needed. Build the smallest thing that genuinely answers the question. That discipline is the real skill this project taught — the SQL syntax was just where it got applied this time.

That's the Beginner Capstone, start to finish — one stakeholder, one clean answer, built the right size the whole way through. From here, the Intermediate project picks up the same company, the same discipline, and a second stakeholder who's about to make things more interesting.
